## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Explain what a class, an object, a generic and a method are.
2. Build an S3 class with a constructor, a validator and methods for `print()` and `summary()`.
3. Write your own generic function.
4. Recognise S4 code and write a simple S4 class and method.
5. Build an R6 class with fields and methods that change the object in place.
6. Choose which system fits a job.

```{webr}
library(R6)
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

## You have used objects all along

Why does `print()` show a data frame as a table, a factor with its levels, and a model with its coefficients? Because `print()` is a **generic** function. It looks at the **class** of its input and calls the matching **method**.

```{webr}
class(hh)
class(factor("a"))
class(lm(household_size ~ 1, data = hh))
```

Some terms:

- A **class** is a type of object, such as `"data.frame"` or `"lm"`.
- An **object** is one value of that class.
- A **generic** is a function whose behaviour depends on the class of its input, such as `print()`, `summary()` or `plot()`.
- A **method** is the version of a generic for one class, such as `print.data.frame()`.

R has several object systems. You will learn the three that matter most:

| System | Style | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| **S3** | simple and informal, built into R | most of base R and the tidyverse |
| **S4** | formal, with defined fields and checks | Bioconductor, some statistics packages |
| **R6** | objects that change in place, like Python or Java | Shiny internals, API clients, simulations |

## S3

### An S3 object is a list with a class

An S3 object is an ordinary R object with a `class` attribute. That is all:

```{webr}
s <- list(name = "Pader household survey", n = 40, districts = c("Gulu", "Arua"))
class(s) <- "survey"
class(s)
unclass(s)    # remove the class to see what is underneath
```

### Constructor and validator

Setting the class by hand works, but nothing stops someone making a broken `survey`. Good practice is to write three functions:

1. A **constructor**, `new_survey()`, that builds the object quickly and checks the basic types.
2. A **validator**, `validate_survey()`, that makes more expensive checks on the values.
3. A **helper**, `survey()`, that users call. It tidies the inputs and calls the other two.

```{webr}
new_survey <- function(data, name) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), is.character(name), length(name) == 1)
  structure(list(data = data, name = name), class = "survey")
}

validate_survey <- function(x) {
  if (!"household_id" %in% names(x$data)) {
    stop("A survey needs a household_id column.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (anyDuplicated(x$data$household_id)) {
    stop("household_id values must be unique.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  x
}

survey <- function(data, name = "Untitled survey") {
  validate_survey(new_survey(data, name))
}

sv <- survey(hh, name = "Northern Uganda household survey")
class(sv)
```

`structure()` creates an object and sets its attributes in one step.

### Methods for existing generics

Printing `sv` now shows the raw list, which is not helpful. Write a `print()` method: a function named `print.survey()`. The name is **generic, a dot, then the class**.

```{webr}
print.survey <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("<survey>", x$name, "\n")
  cat(nrow(x$data), "households,", length(unique(x$data$district)), "districts\n")
  invisible(x)
}

sv
```

A few conventions:

- Methods take the same arguments as the generic. `print()` has `x` and `...`, so `print.survey()` must too.
- A `print()` method returns its input invisibly, so `y <- print(x)` works and nothing prints twice.

Add a `summary()` method the same way:

```{webr}
summary.survey <- function(object, ...) {
  table(object$data$district)
}
summary(sv)
```

### Your own generic

To make a new generic, write a function that calls `UseMethod()`. Then write methods for the classes you need, and a `default` method for everything else:

```{webr}
coverage <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("coverage")

coverage.survey <- function(x, column, ...) {
  mean(!is.na(x$data[[column]]))
}

coverage.default <- function(x, ...) {
  mean(!is.na(x))
}

coverage(sv, "monthly_income_ugx")    # uses coverage.survey()
coverage(c(1, NA, 3, 4))              # uses coverage.default()
```

`UseMethod("coverage")` looks at the class of the first argument and calls `coverage.<class>()`. If there is no such method, it calls `coverage.default()`. If there is no default either, you get an error.

### Inheritance

An object can have several classes. R tries them in order:

```{webr}
panel <- sv
class(panel) <- c("panel_survey", "survey")
panel                # no print.panel_survey(), so print.survey() is used

print.panel_survey <- function(x, ...) {
  cat("(panel survey: households are visited more than once)\n")
  NextMethod()       # then carry on with the next class, survey
}
panel
```

`NextMethod()` calls the method for the next class in the list. It lets a subclass add to its parent's behaviour instead of copying it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## See the methods for a class or generic
`methods(class = "survey")` lists the methods for a class. `methods("print")` lists every `print()` method, which is a long list.
:::

```{webr}
methods(class = "survey")
```

## S4

S4 is a stricter version of the same idea. A class has defined **slots** (fields) with fixed types, and R checks them when you create an object. You will mostly **read** S4 code in other packages, so learn to recognise it.

```{webr}
setClass("District", representation(name = "character", households = "numeric"))

gulu <- new("District", name = "Gulu", households = 11)
gulu
gulu@name             # slots use @, not $
isVirtualClass("District")
```

Giving a slot the wrong type is an error straight away:

```{webr}
new("District", name = "Arua", households = "ten") # Error expected: households must be numeric
```

Generics and methods are created with `setGeneric()` and `setMethod()`:

```{webr}
setGeneric("describe", function(obj) standardGeneric("describe"))

setMethod("describe", "District", function(obj) {
  paste0(obj@name, ": ", obj@households, " households")
})

describe(gulu)
```

You can add a **validity** function that runs every time an object is created:

```{webr}
setClass("Site",
  representation(name = "character", visits = "numeric"),
  validity = function(object) {
    if (any(object@visits < 0)) "visits cannot be negative" else TRUE
  }
)
new("Site", name = "Pabbo", visits = 3)
```

The details of S4 go further than this lesson. Use S4 when you are contributing to a package that already uses it, such as those in Bioconductor.

## R6

S3 and S4 objects follow R's usual **copy-on-modify** rule: change a copy, and the original stays the same (Day 17). R6 objects are different. They are built on environments, so they are **modified in place**, and every name that points to the object sees the change. This is called **reference semantics**.

That makes R6 the right tool for objects that hold changing **state**: a connection to a database, a queue of jobs, a running simulation, a progress tracker.

### A first R6 class

```{webr}
Tracker <- R6Class("Tracker",
  public = list(
    target = NULL,
    done = 0,

    initialize = function(target) {
      stopifnot(is.numeric(target), target > 0)
      self$target <- target
    },

    record = function(n = 1) {
      self$done <- self$done + n
      invisible(self)
    },

    progress = function() {
      paste0(self$done, " of ", self$target, " interviews (", round(100 * self$done / self$target), "%)")
    }
  )
)

gulu_team <- Tracker$new(target = 15)
gulu_team$record(4)
gulu_team$progress()
```

- `R6Class()` defines the class. Its `public` list holds **fields** (values) and **methods** (functions).
- `Tracker$new()` creates an object and runs `initialize()`.
- Inside methods, `self` is the object itself.
- Methods that change the object return `invisible(self)`, so calls can be **chained**:

```{webr}
gulu_team$record(2)$record(3)$progress()
```

### Reference semantics

```{webr}
copy_of_team <- gulu_team    # NOT a copy: both names point to the same object
copy_of_team$record(6)
gulu_team$progress()         # changed too

real_copy <- gulu_team$clone()
real_copy$record(100)
gulu_team$progress()         # unchanged
```

Use `$clone()` when you really want a separate copy.

### Private fields

Fields in `private` cannot be reached from outside the object. Use them to protect values that should only change through methods:

```{webr}
Account <- R6Class("Account",
  public = list(
    deposit = function(amount) {
      stopifnot(amount > 0)
      private$balance <- private$balance + amount
      invisible(self)
    },
    get_balance = function() private$balance
  ),
  private = list(balance = 0)
)

acc <- Account$new()
acc$deposit(50000)$deposit(25000)
acc$get_balance()
acc$balance              # NULL: private fields are hidden
```

## Which system should I use?

| If you need… | Use |
|---|---|
| a new type of result with nice `print()` and `summary()` output | **S3**. It is simple and is what most R users expect. |
| strict types and validation, or you are extending an S4 package | **S4** |
| an object whose state changes over time, shared by several parts of your code | **R6** |
| none of these | a plain list or data frame, and functions |

Start with S3. Most packages never need more.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
A custom Excel table with fixed columns and data validation is like an S4 class: you cannot put text in a number column. A shared workbook that several people edit is like an R6 object: everyone sees the same, changing copy. Saving a copy of a file before you change it is copy-on-modify.
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: An S3 constructor

Write `new_money()`. It should check that `amount` is numeric, then return `amount` with the class `"money"` and an attribute `currency`. Use `structure()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_constructor
new_money <- function(amount, currency = "UGX") {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(amount))
  structure(amount, class = ______, currency = ______)
}
m <- new_money(c(25000, 7500))
class(m)
attr(m, "currency")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex18_constructor"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The class is the text `"money"`. The currency attribute is the `currency` argument.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex18_constructor"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
new_money <- function(amount, currency = "UGX") {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(amount))
  structure(amount, class = "money", currency = currency)
}
m <- new_money(c(25000, 7500))
class(m)
attr(m, "currency")
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_constructor
#| check: true
fails_text <- tryCatch({ new_money("a"); FALSE }, error = function(e) TRUE)
x <- tryCatch(new_money(10, "KES"), error = function(e) NULL)
if (!exists("new_money") || !is.function(new_money)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create a function called new_money.")
} else if (is.null(x) || !identical(class(x), "money")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The object's class should be \"money\".")
} else if (!identical(attr(x, "currency"), "KES")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Set the currency attribute from the argument: currency = currency.")
} else if (!fails_text) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "new_money(\"a\") should stop with an error. Keep the stopifnot() check.")
} else if (!identical(unclass(x)[1], 10)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The amount should stay the same underneath the class.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. You have made a new S3 class.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: A `format()` method

Write a `format()` method for the `"money"` class. It should return text such as `"UGX 25,000"`: the currency, a space, and the amount with a comma for thousands. A `print()` method that uses it is already written.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_method
#| setup: true
new_money <- function(amount, currency = "UGX") {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(amount))
  structure(amount, class = "money", currency = currency)
}
print.money <- function(x, ...) {
  print(format(x), quote = FALSE)
  invisible(x)
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_method
______ <- function(x, ...) {
  paste(attr(x, "currency"), format(unclass(x), big.mark = ","))
}
format(new_money(c(25000, 7500)))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex18_method"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
A method's name is the generic, a dot and the class: `format.money`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex18_method"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
format.money <- function(x, ...) {
  paste(attr(x, "currency"), format(unclass(x), big.mark = ","))
}
format(new_money(c(25000, 7500)))
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_method
#| check: true
if (!exists("format.money") || !is.function(format.money)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Name the method format.money: the generic, a dot, then the class.")
} else {
  out <- format(new_money(c(25000, 7500)))
  if (identical(trimws(out), c("UGX 25,000", "UGX 7,500")) || identical(gsub(" +", " ", out), c("UGX 25,000", "UGX 7,500"))) {
    list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. format() now dispatches to your method, and print.money() uses it.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = paste0("format() gave ", paste(out, collapse = ", "), ". Expected UGX 25,000 and UGX 7,500."))
  }
}
```

### Exercise 3: A new generic

Create a generic `area()` with `UseMethod()`, and two methods: `area.square()` returns `side^2` and `area.circle()` returns `pi * radius^2`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_generic
area <- function(shape) ______("area")
area.square <- function(shape) shape$side^2
area.circle <- function(shape) ______

sq <- structure(list(side = 3), class = "square")
ci <- structure(list(radius = 1), class = "circle")
area(sq)
area(ci)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex18_generic"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The generic's body is `UseMethod("area")`. The circle method uses `shape$radius`: `pi * shape$radius^2`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex18_generic"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
area <- function(shape) UseMethod("area")
area.square <- function(shape) shape$side^2
area.circle <- function(shape) pi * shape$radius^2

sq <- structure(list(side = 3), class = "square")
ci <- structure(list(radius = 1), class = "circle")
area(sq)
area(ci)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_generic
#| check: true
a1 <- tryCatch(area(structure(list(side = 4), class = "square")), error = function(e) NULL)
a2 <- tryCatch(area(structure(list(radius = 2), class = "circle")), error = function(e) NULL)
if (!exists("area") || !any(grepl("UseMethod", deparse(body(area))))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The generic area() should call UseMethod(\"area\").")
} else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(a1, 16))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "area() of a square with side 4 should be 16.")
} else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(a2, pi * 4))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "area() of a circle with radius 2 should be pi * 2^2. Use pi * shape$radius^2.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. One generic, two methods, chosen by class.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: An S4 class

Define an S4 class `"Crop"` with two slots: `name` (character) and `yield_kg` (numeric). Create an object `maize` with name `"maize"` and yield `1200`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_s4
setClass("Crop", representation(name = ______, yield_kg = ______))
maize <- new("Crop", name = "maize", yield_kg = 1200)
maize@yield_kg
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex18_s4"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Each slot type is given as text: `name = "character"` and `yield_kg = "numeric"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex18_s4"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
setClass("Crop", representation(name = "character", yield_kg = "numeric"))
maize <- new("Crop", name = "maize", yield_kg = 1200)
maize@yield_kg
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_s4
#| check: true
if (!isClass("Crop")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Define the class with setClass(\"Crop\", ...).")
} else {
  slots <- getSlots("Crop")
  rejects_text <- tryCatch({ new("Crop", name = "beans", yield_kg = "lots"); FALSE }, error = function(e) TRUE)
  if (!identical(unname(slots[c("name", "yield_kg")]), c("character", "numeric"))) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "The slots should be name = \"character\" and yield_kg = \"numeric\".")
  } else if (!exists("maize") || !is(maize, "Crop") || !identical(maize@yield_kg, 1200)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create maize with new(\"Crop\", name = \"maize\", yield_kg = 1200).")
  } else if (!rejects_text) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "A text yield should be rejected. Check the slot type.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. S4 checks the slot types for you.")
  }
}
```

### Exercise 5: An R6 class

Complete the R6 class `Queue`. `add()` should append `item` to the `items` field and return `invisible(self)`. `size()` should return the number of items.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_r6
#| setup: true
library(R6)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_r6
Queue <- R6Class("Queue",
  public = list(
    items = list(),
    add = function(item) {
      self$items <- c(self$items, list(item))
      ______
    },
    size = function() ______
  )
)
q <- Queue$new()
q$add("HH001")$add("HH002")
q$size()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex18_r6"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Return `invisible(self)` so calls can be chained. The size is `length(self$items)`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex18_r6"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
Queue <- R6Class("Queue",
  public = list(
    items = list(),
    add = function(item) {
      self$items <- c(self$items, list(item))
      invisible(self)
    },
    size = function() length(self$items)
  )
)
q <- Queue$new()
q$add("HH001")$add("HH002")
q$size()
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex18_r6
#| check: true
if (!exists("Queue") || !inherits(Queue, "R6ClassGenerator")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Define Queue with R6Class().")
} else {
  q2 <- Queue$new()
  chained <- tryCatch({ q2$add("a")$add("b"); TRUE }, error = function(e) FALSE)
  if (!chained) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "Chaining failed. add() should end with invisible(self).")
  } else if (!identical(q2$size(), 2L)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, message = "After two adds, size() should return 2. Use length(self$items).")
  } else {
    q3 <- q2
    q3$add("c")
    if (!identical(q2$size(), 3L)) {
      list(correct = FALSE, message = "Something is off with the items field.")
    } else {
      list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. And because R6 objects are references, adding through q3 also changed q2.")
    }
  }
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Getting the method name wrong.** It is `generic.class`, such as `print.survey`. `printsurvey` or `survey.print` are never called.
- **Method arguments that do not match the generic.** `print.survey <- function(s)` breaks when `print()` passes `x`. Copy the generic's arguments, including `...`.
- **Using `$` on S4 objects.** S4 slots use `@`.
- **Treating an R6 object like an ordinary value.** `b <- a` does not copy it. Use `a$clone()`.
- **Forgetting `self$`** inside R6 methods. `done <- done + 1` creates a local variable. `self$done <- self$done + 1` changes the field.
- **Reaching for R6 when a function would do.** Objects that change in place are harder to reason about. Use them only when you need shared, changing state.

## Summary

- Generics such as `print()` and `summary()` call a different method for each class.
- **S3:** an object is a value with a `class` attribute. Write a constructor, a validator and a helper. Methods are named `generic.class`. New generics call `UseMethod()`. `NextMethod()` passes on to the parent class.
- **S4:** formal classes with typed slots, created with `setClass()` and `new()`. Slots use `@`. Methods use `setGeneric()` and `setMethod()`.
- **R6:** classes built with `R6Class()`. Objects are modified in place, use `self` inside methods, and can have `private` fields. Copy with `$clone()`.
- Start with S3. Use S4 for strict types and R6 for shared, changing state.

**Next:** on Day 19 you will measure and speed up slow code.
